title: The Paradox of Participation Versus Misinformation: Social Media, Political Engagement, and the Spread of Misinformation
screen_reason: Two-wave national online panel survey in Chile (wave 1 April 2017, N = 1,007). Respondents were shown 10 false claims circulating online and reported, for each, whether they were unaware of it, aware but had not shared it, or aware and had shared it. Table 1 gives per-claim familiarity (26-92%) and sharing (3-25%) shares, and the text gives the headline figures: more than 75% were aware of at least four claims, and each claim was shared on average by 12% of participants. These are RECALL exposure and RECALL sharing shares with a population denominator. The credibility/misperception results are belief measures and are excluded.

estimates.platform: online (statements described as stories circulating online in the past 12 months); social media sharing
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents aware of at least four of the ten false claims presented
estimates.value_raw: more than 75% of respondents reported being aware of at least four claims
estimates.denominator: 1,007 Chilean online panel respondents (TrenDigital panel matched to population parameters on gender, age and region), wave 1
estimates.definition: Respondent reported having been aware of the claim (whether or not they shared it) for four or more of the ten false statements presented
estimates.misinfo_def: a category of claim for which there is at least substantial disagreement (or even consensus rejection) when judged as to truth value among the widest feasible range of observers
estimates.source_quote: In wave-1, more than 75% of respondents reported being aware of at least four claims, especially those related to the great wildfires of 2017 and scientific myths related to vaccines.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Awareness is self-reported; the ten statements were selected by the authors as false claims that had actually circulated online in Chile in the previous 12 months, covering disasters, science and government affairs; respondents were not told the statements were false, to reduce social-desirability bias
estimates.moderator_quote: We presented respondents with a list of 10 statements covering the three issue domains explained earlier (see Table 1). To reduce social desirability biases, we did not specify whether the statements were true or false.
estimates.notes: Wave 1 taken as the representative time point (Table 1 is wave-1 only). The value is a lower bound as printed ('more than 75%'), recorded at 75. Topic coded 'other' because the ten claims span three domains (disasters, science including vaccines, government affairs) and no single topic code fits the set.

estimates.measure_type: average % of respondents who report having shared a given false claim (mean across the ten claims)
estimates.value_raw: Each claim was shared, on average, by 12% of participants.
estimates.denominator: 1,007 Chilean online panel respondents (TrenDigital panel matched to population parameters on gender, age and region), wave 1
estimates.definition: Respondent reported having been aware of the claim and having shared it; averaged over the ten false claims
estimates.misinfo_def: a category of claim for which there is at least substantial disagreement (or even consensus rejection) when judged as to truth value among the widest feasible range of observers
estimates.source_quote: Each claim was shared, on average, by 12% of participants.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Sharing is self-reported on a three-option per-claim item (unaware / aware but not shared / aware and shared); index of misinformation sharing KR-20 = 0.73 in wave 1
estimates.moderator_quote: For each statement, respondents were asked whether they had: (a) not been aware of it, (b) been aware of it but had not shared it, or (c) been aware of it and had shared it.
estimates.notes: The 12% is the paper's own average across the ten per-claim sharing shares (Table 1 range 3-25%), not the share of respondents who shared any claim, which the paper does not report. Marked borderline because it is a mean of proportions rather than a single part/whole share; it is stated verbatim, so it satisfies R8, but the underlying denominator is the same 1,007 respondents for each of the ten claims.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) the ten per-claim familiarity shares in Table 1 (92, 81, 75, 74, 70, 68, 60, 42, 32, 26) and the ten per-claim sharing shares (14, 20, 12, 25, 17, 10, 6, 10, 6, 3) — these are the item-level components of the two headline rows above, all on the same 1,007-respondent denominator, and must never be summed across claims (R8); I kept the paper's own summary figures instead of ten near-duplicate rows (R4); (b) the domain averages for sharing (disasters 12%, health 16%, government affairs 6%) — subgroup averages of the same item; (c) all belief/credibility figures (average 24% find claims very or extremely credible; 18% vaccines-autism; nearly half for GMOs; the per-claim 'believes claim is accurate' column) — belief in false claims is explicitly excluded; (d) the misperception and misinformation-sharing scale means (M = 2.54; M = 1.19 of 10) — scale means, not shares; (e) figures cited from other studies (Bode and Vraga 11% and 51%; Reuters Institute 64% of Chileans preferring social media news) — barred by R8. Worth a human's attention: the ten statements mix genuinely false claims with contested science claims ('some vaccines have side effects that may be worse than the very illnesses they are trying to prevent'), so the numerator's veracity strictness is uneven across items.

rob.design: Two-wave national online panel survey in Chile administered by TrenDigital (Pontificia Universidad Catolica de Chile), frame matched to population parameters on gender, age and region. Wave 1 April 2017: 5,000 panellists contacted via Qualtrics email, 1,007 responses, 20% completion rate. 127 dropped for incomplete key variables and 9 for speeding; of the 871 remaining, 451 completed wave 2 in June 2018 (48% attrition). Misinformation measured by a 10-item battery of false claims with a three-option awareness/sharing item plus a 5-point credibility item; sharing index KR-20 = 0.73 (wave 1), 0.65 (wave 2); misperception scale alpha = 0.78 (wave 1). Self-report throughout; no behavioural validation.
rob.item6_quote: In the current study, we use Southwell et al.'s (2018, 3) definition: "a category of claim for which there is at least substantial disagreement (or even consensus rejection) when judged as to truth value among the widest feasible range of observers."
rob.item10_quote: In wave-1, more than 75% of respondents reported being aware of at least four claims, especially those related to the great wildfires of 2017 and scientific myths related to vaccines.
